blocks.text: Comparative anatomists study the structure of fossils and living organisms, looking for similarities that indicate evolutionary relationships. This reveals two types of evolution.

items: Divergent evolution: homologous structures are similar in structure but different in function (homology). Organisms with homologous structures share a common ancestor and evolved to use them for different functions; vertebrate forelimbs share the same arrangement of bones although they are used for flight (birds and bats), swimming (whales and dolphins), running (horses), climbing (tree lizards) or swinging from branches.

Convergent evolution: analogous organs are similar in function but different in structure, and evolved in different kinds of organisms from different ancestors. The wing of a bird and the wing of an insect both allow flight but are not homologous; their similarity only reflects that flight needs a broad, flat surface.

blocks.alt: Top: the forelimbs of a human, bat, whale and bird drawn as bones in matching colours, blue humerus, green radius and ulna, yellow wrist bones and red hand bones, showing the same pattern used for grasping, flying, swimming and flying. Bottom: a bird wing of bones and feathers beside an insect wing of thin membrane, both used for flight.
blocks.caption: Homologous forelimbs and analogous wings (original diagram after Figure 24.5).
blocks.long_description: Homologous structures have the same basic structure but different functions. The forelimbs of vertebrates share an arrangement of bones, upper arm, forearm, wrist and hand, although they are used for flight in birds and bats, swimming in whales, running, climbing or grasping; this shows descent from a common ancestor followed by divergent evolution. Analogous structures do the same job but are built differently: the wings of birds and insects both allow flight, but a bird wing has bones and feathers and an insect wing is a thin membrane. Their similarity reflects the needs of flight, not common ancestry, and is an example of convergent evolution.

blocks.text: Organisms often keep structures that have lost their usefulness; these poorly developed structures are vestigial. Some snakes, such as boas and pythons, have tiny remnants of hind-limb (pelvic) bones from their reptile ancestors. Such remnants of once-useful structures are clear signs of evolution.

blocks.title: Vestigial structures in humans
blocks.text: There are about 90 vestigial structures in the human body, for example the vermiform appendix (a vestige of the caecum), the coccyx or tailbone (the remnant of a tail), wisdom teeth (vestigial third molars that ancestors used to grind plant food) and the ear muscles, which are minimally developed though some people can move their ears.
